source.version: IJCAI-25 proceedings paper, Special Track on Human-Centred AI, printed pages 10280-10288 (PDF pp. 1-9). The document bears the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-25) proceedings header; no separate revision date is given.
source.title_on_document: Creative Momentum Transfer: How Timing and Labeling of AI Suggestions Shape Iterative Human Ideation

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or appendix is identified in the complete PDF. The main text contains the reported tests and Table 1 contains standard errors for moderator slopes; no external source of missing treatment-effect precision is named.

paper_design_summary: Adults were randomized to a control receiving no external suggestions or to GPT-4 suggestions introduced early or late and explicitly AI-labeled or unlabeled during two rounds of proposing solutions to urban plastic pollution on a web platform. Experts rated creativity and its components, and embedding comparisons measured each participant's alignment with the AI suggestions. The paper also describes a preparatory stimulus pilot and qualitative interviews with a subset of the main experimental sample.

studies.label: Main five-condition, two-round plastic-pollution ideation experiment

assignment.what_was_assigned: People were assigned to Control, Early-AI-Labeled, Early-AI-Unlabeled, Late-AI-Labeled, or Late-AI-Unlabeled. The timing and labeling manipulation is between participants; the same participants completed both rounds. Allocation method and concealment are not described. The online_rct label follows the stated web-platform administration, although recruitment channel and physical setting are not specified.

participants.exclusions: Reported analyzed sample after the seven specified exclusions: 247 adults from 254 initially enrolled; exclusions were for failed attention checks or cursory responses (PDF p. 3 (printed p. 10282), Section 3.1). Section 3.6 additionally describes removing outliers above three standard deviations and incomplete responses, without giving counts or saying whether these were the same seven exclusions (PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283)). The one-way ANOVAs repeatedly report F(4, 237), inconsistent with the stated sample under the described five-group model (PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Section 4.1). The exact analyzed total and arm counts after all screening are therefore unconfirmed and left null; no replacement headcount is inferred from degrees of freedom. The timing of the seven exclusions relative to assignment and original allocation totals are also unreported, so randomized counts remain null. The reported post-exclusion sample and participant-score ANOVA degrees of freedom both support substantially more than 50 analyzed people, although they do not settle the exact denominator.
participants.who: Adult convenience sample. Demographic screening sought diversity in age, gender, and education, but the recruitment frame, occupational/student composition, and country are not reported. A population category cannot be confirmed from adult age or web administration. Twelve participants from the main experiment were selected for qualitative follow-up, not an independent additional sample (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1-3.4; PDF p. 7, Section 5).
participants.quote: A total of 254 adult participants were initially enrolled, and seven were removed for failing attention checks or offering cursory responses, resulting in a final sample size of 247.

ai_tool.how_used: Participants received two or three pre-generated suggestions displayed with the task prompt, in the early or late round according to assignment. Each suggestion was 30-50 words, Flesch-Kincaid reading level 10-12, and pre-rated for creativity M = 5.3 on a 7-point scale. Authors lightly edited GPT-4 outputs after pilot feedback to standardize style and remove inaccuracies. Labeled suggestions had a bold AI-generated heading and a distinctive icon; unlabeled suggestions were attributed to others. No participant chatbot interaction is described (p. 3, section 3.3).

task.description: Propose innovative solutions to reduce urban plastic pollution, feasible within the next five years and meaningful at community level; then refine, expand, combine, or develop new solutions in Round 2. A minimum of 50 words was required after each round. A brick Alternative Uses Task preceded the ideation task as a baseline fluency measure, not an AI-treatment outcome (pp. 3-4, sections 3.3-3.4).
task.duration: Two 5-7-minute ideation rounds in the same session; pre-study assessment 8-10 minutes and post-task evaluation 4-5 minutes. Baseline brick AUT lasted two minutes; the selected follow-up interviews lasted 15-20 minutes (pp. 3-4, section 3.4 and Figure 1).

outcomes.name: Expert-rated overall creativity of the ideation submission, including change across rounds
outcomes.measure_detail: Modified Consensual Assessment Technique. Three experts in environmental policy or innovation management independently assessed final ideas on novelty, usefulness, and originality using 7-point scales; intraclass correlation >= 0.80. The formula combining these ratings into overall creativity and the aggregation across experts/ideas are not specified (PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Section 3.5). The reported analyses use participant creativity scores; repeated measures are within participants. Section 3.5 describes final submissions, while Section 4.4 also analyzes Round 1 scores without separately describing their rating procedure. Final levels and round-to-round changes are retained as one outcome. Table 1 reports slopes of baseline AUT fluency on final creativity, not treatment effects: Control slope -0.012, SE 0.031, p = 0.687; Early-AI-Labeled 0.117, SE 0.035, p = 0.005; Early-AI-Unlabeled 0.159, SE 0.033, p < .001; Late-AI-Labeled 0.093, SE 0.037, p = 0.029; Late-AI-Unlabeled 0.118, SE 0.036, p = 0.005. The baseline-creativity-by-condition interaction is F(4, 237) = 4.42, p = .002; trust moderation is reported as p > .17 (PDF p. 5 (printed p. 10284), Section 4.3, Table 1 and Figure 2d). These moderator statistics are not standardized AI effects. Figure 2 shows shaded 95% confidence intervals without numerical bounds (PDF p. 5 (printed p. 10284), Figure 2 caption). Timing qualification: Early-AI Round 1 and Late-AI Round 2 explicitly include GPT-4 suggestions and support with_ai. Control receives no suggestions in either round, and Late-AI Round 1 is unassisted. For Early-AI Round 2, the paper states only that there were no new external inputs; it does not establish whether earlier suggestions remained accessible or were withdrawn. Early-AI final-output AI availability and question are therefore unconfirmed: neither with_ai nor after_ai is established. Because this outcome entry includes final results involving Early-AI participants, its shared question and ai_available_when_produced fields are null; this uncertainty must not be represented as confirmed mixed availability. Late-AI final outputs remain confirmed with_ai within the retained results (PDF p. 3 (printed p. 10282), Sections 3.3-3.4; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Section 3.4 and Figure 1).

contrasts.reported: Early-AI-Labeled M = 6.01, SD = 0.48; Control M = 4.94. Descriptives are incomplete: Control SD and a numerical pairwise test, interval, or effect size are not supplied. contrasts.reported: Both Early-AI groups are reported to surpass the Late-AI groups in final overall creativity. This records the stated timing comparison, not a reconstructed pooled-arm estimate; no numerical timing coefficient, SE, or exact pairwise p-value is provided.
F(4, 237) = 37.54, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .38. This is the five-condition omnibus ANOVA, not an effect size or test for any one treatment-control contrast.

Creativity increases up to +0.88; t = -19.69, p < .001, d = 1.73. The text does not identify whether these statistics describe one Late-AI arm or the two arms together. Early-AI-Labeled improved by +0.17 and Control by +0.14. A repeated-measures ANOVA is described as confirming larger Late-AI improvements, but no F statistic or precision for the between-condition difference in change is printed. The reported d is a within-participant change effect, not a randomized between-arm effect. Source inconsistency: in Figure 2e, the Early-AI-Labeled creativity trajectory is steeper than either Late-AI trajectory under the shared legend, conflicting with Section 4.4 attribution of the largest gains to Late-AI. The change statistics here are transcribed from the prose; no graph values are estimated, and the group attribution requires author clarification (PDF p. 5 (printed p. 10284), Section 4.4 and Figure 2e).

outcomes.name: Semantic distance of participants' submissions from the supplied GPT-4 suggestions, including change across rounds
outcomes.measure_detail: Each submission was embedded with text-embedding-ada-002 and compared with each GPT-4 suggestion using cosine similarity. Results are reported as semantic distance, with lower distance indicating stronger overlap (PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Section 3.5). The transformation from cosine similarity to distance and the aggregation across suggestions are not specified. The paper analyzes a semantic-distance score for each participant submission; the number of underlying text pairs is not reported. This is alignment with AI exemplars, not similarity between different people, so it is not coded diversity or across_people. Final levels and within-participant changes are grouped as the same output measure. A process correlation with perceived external influence is r = -0.35, p < .001 (PDF p. 5 (printed p. 10284), Section 4.2 and Figure 2c); that self-report is not a separate scored-output outcome. Directions below refer to the reported distance scale; no signs or effect sizes have been recalculated. Timing qualification: Early-AI Round 1 and Late-AI Round 2 explicitly include GPT-4 suggestions and support with_ai. Control receives no suggestions in either round, and Late-AI Round 1 is unassisted. For Early-AI Round 2, the paper states only that there were no new external inputs; it does not establish whether earlier suggestions remained accessible or were withdrawn. Early-AI final-output AI availability and question are therefore unconfirmed: neither with_ai nor after_ai is established. Because this outcome entry includes final results involving Early-AI participants, its shared question and ai_available_when_produced fields are null; this uncertainty must not be represented as confirmed mixed availability. Late-AI final outputs remain confirmed with_ai within the retained results (PDF p. 3 (printed p. 10282), Sections 3.3-3.4; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Section 3.4 and Figure 1).

Descriptives are incomplete: no SDs or numerical pairwise effect/precision are printed. Lower values mean stronger alignment to AI suggestions.

studies.label: Preparatory pilot for GPT-4 suggestion selection and editing

assignment.what_was_assigned: The paper describes a stimulus-checking pilot, without an allocation scheme, comparison conditions, or a human AI-assisted production task.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or participant flow are described.
participants.who: A pilot is reported as n = 15, but the paragraph does not explicitly identify that n as people rather than stimuli/ratings and gives no participant description. A people count is therefore left null; the printed n is preserved in the quote. This pilot is not added to the main experimental sample.
participants.quote: Prior to finalizing these AI prompts, we conducted a small pilot study (n = 15) to verify that the suggestions were consistent in length, clarity, and perceived originality.

ai_tool.how_used: AI-generated suggestions were checked before the main experiment and lightly edited based on pilot feedback. They are the material being evaluated, not documented assistance for a human creative-production task (PDF p. 3 (printed p. 10282), Section 3.3).

task.description: Check consistency of AI suggestions in length, clarity, and perceived originality. Section 3.3 also says the suggestions were prerated for creativity (M = 5.3 on a 7-point scale), but does not clearly attribute that statistic to the pilot or specify the rating sample (PDF p. 3 (printed p. 10282)). No eligible outcome on human-produced creative work is reported.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of participants from another paper is stated. The qualitative interviews follow the main experiment and use a subset of its participants. Whether the stimulus pilot overlapped with the main sample is not stated.

eligibility.reason: S1 explicitly randomly assigns people to GPT-4 suggestion timing/labeling conditions or a no-suggestion Control for their own ideation (PDF p. 3 (printed p. 10282), Sections 3.1-3.4). The reported analyzed sample after seven specified exclusions is 247 adults, with reported arm counts of 50, 49, 49, 50, and 49 (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1). Further unquantified screening and one-way ANOVA F(4, 237) leave the exact analyzed total and arm counts unresolved, so those numeric fields are null; nevertheless the reported sample and the participant-score ANOVA degrees of freedom independently support a sample well above 50 (PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Sections 3.5-3.6 and 4.1). Three domain experts rate the novelty, usefulness, and originality of participants' produced submissions, with overall creativity analyzed in Section 4.1 (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.5 and 4.1). Late-AI participants explicitly receive GPT-4 suggestions while producing the final scored output (PDF p. 4, Section 3.4), so unresolved Early-AI Round 2 access does not affect the three eligibility criteria. The stimulus pilot, interview subset, raters, and repeated rounds are not added to the participant count. S1 remains core eligible; S2 does not independently qualify.

one_line_finding: Final expert-rated creativity was higher in Early-AI-Labeled (M = 6.01, SD = 0.48) than Control (M = 4.94), with an omnibus condition effect of F(4, 237) = 37.54, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .38 (PDF p. 4 (printed p. 10283), Section 4.1).
open_questions: Which population category applies, and what recruitment frame, occupational/student composition, country, and supervised versus remote setting were used? The PDF reports only an adult convenience sample and web-platform administration. This also covers the unresolved reconciliation difference studies.S1.participants.population (PDF p. 3, Sections 3.1-3.3; PDF p. 7, Section 5).

Were the seven stated exclusions before or after random assignment, and were the outlier/incomplete-response removals the same exclusions? Original randomized totals and arm allocation/exclusion counts remain unknown (PDF p. 3, Section 3.1; PDF p. 4, Section 3.6).

What exact analyzed total and per-arm counts, screening decisions, or model specification reconcile the reported analyzed sample after seven exclusions of 247 with the repeated one-way ANOVA degrees of freedom F(4, 237)? Exact analyzed count fields are null; the reported counts remain qualified prose, and no alternative headcount is inferred (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1, 3.6 and 4.1).

Were Early-AI suggestions still accessible during Round 2? No new external inputs does not establish withdrawal. The shared question and availability fields for outcomes containing Early-AI final results are null; Late-AI final outputs and Early-AI Round 1 are confirmed with_ai (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3.4 and Figure 1).

How were dimension, idea, and individual-rater scores combined into participant creativity, and how were Round 1 submissions rated? Complete arm SDs, model-specific counts, numerical pairwise effects, and precision also remain unreported (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.5-4.4 and Figure 2).

How was cosine similarity transformed into semantic distance and aggregated across AI suggestions? These comparisons concern participant submissions versus supplied AI suggestions, not comparisons across people (PDF p. 4, Section 3.5).

Which Late-AI arm or aggregation supplies the increase up to +0.88, t = -19.69, d = 1.73, and semantic-distance change -0.23? How should the claim of largest Late-AI creativity gains be reconciled with the steeper Early-AI-Labeled trajectory in Figure 2e? The prose numbers are retained without estimating values from the graph (PDF p. 5, Section 4.4 and Figure 2e).

Does the pilot n = 15 count people, did any pilot participants enter the main experiment, and does the prerated stimulus creativity M = 5.3 come from that pilot? None is specified; no pilot count is added to S1 (PDF p. 3, Section 3.3).
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently checking all three challenge files against the source. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical review evidence; the corrected fields and final object govern the final screening decision. Read all 320 markdown lines and extracted the text of all 9 PDF pages, including all references; no appendix is included. Every retained numerical fact was checked against the PDF. Table 1 was recovered separately with PyMuPDF find_tables using a clipped text strategy. Locators use PDF page numbers, with printed pagination where useful. S1 is the main randomized experiment. S2 is the explicitly named stimulus pilot; its n = 15 is not assumed to count analyzed people and is not added to S1. The interviews are a subset of S1. All five supported output measures are retained: overall creativity, novelty, usefulness, originality, and semantic distance to AI suggestions. Repeated-round versions remain within their corresponding outcomes; moderator slopes are not treatment effects. Novelty and originality stay separate because the paper rates and tests them separately. No outcome measures similarity between different people. Late-AI final outputs support with_ai; the unknown continued access for Early-AI is preserved, without a confirmed after_ai outcome. The shared question and ai_available_when_produced fields for all five retained outcome entries are null because each includes unresolved Early-AI final results; the confirmed with_ai timing of Late-AI final outputs and Early-AI Round 1 is preserved in measure_detail. Unknown continued access is not coded as confirmed mixed availability. Participant is the analysis-unit coding for the reported condition scores and within-participant repeated measures; the exact aggregation of multiple ideas/ratings is not provided. The exact analyzed total and every analyzed arm count are null. The reported analyzed counts after the seven specified exclusions remain in qualified prose because Section 3.6 additional screening and Section 4.1 ANOVA degrees of freedom do not establish the actual analysis denominators. The initially enrolled count is not treated as the randomized total. online_rct follows the explicit web-platform delivery, while an online panel, remote participation, or supervised setting cannot be confirmed. No primary outcome, preregistration, supplement link, data repository, code repository, or reuse of another paper sample is stated. Company involvement is the author affiliation on PDF p. 1. Omnibus ANOVAs have separate comparison_type other entries, and null direction where no directional contrast is defined; null does not imply a null effect. Originality no_clear_difference refers to its non-significant omnibus test. The timing comparisons consistently use Late-AI as treatment and Early-AI as reference, a coding convention rather than a claim that the paper declares a default arm. Empty statistics_available arrays on the descriptive Early-AI-Labeled versus Control entries mean no complete enumerated statistical package is available: the printed means and any available SD remain in reported. The Late-AI semantic-distance change also has an empty array because a raw change without SE does not qualify as mean_difference_se, and its printed number is not figure-only. Figure-only flags elsewhere mean the numerical levels/contrasts are not printed; accompanying qualitative statements are described in reported. The manuscript effect-size labels and signs are transcribed unchanged; no effects, CIs, SDs, alternative sample counts, or graph values were calculated. Baseline AUT fluency/trust, perceived external influence, creative self-efficacy, source recognition, response times, and interview themes are not additional scored-output outcomes. The process statistics supplied only in B are retained here as context: perceived external influence M = 5.36 vs. 4.39, t = 7.22, p < .001, d = 1.03; 64% of unlabeled participants suspected an AI source (PDF p. 5, Section 4.2). Reconciliation counts substantive field omissions/coding differences, including treatment-reference orientation, but not synonymous descriptions, alternate arm punctuation, empty versus null representations of the same unknown, or relocation of facts already documented identically elsewhere. Shared source limitations are retained in open_questions and agreed_fields_checked; n_unresolved counts unresolved differences between A and B. Source inconsistency: in Figure 2e, the Early-AI-Labeled creativity trajectory is steeper than either Late-AI trajectory under the shared legend, conflicting with Section 4.4 attribution of the largest gains to Late-AI. The change statistics here are transcribed from the prose; no graph values are estimated, and the group attribution requires author clarification (PDF p. 5 (printed p. 10284), Section 4.4 and Figure 2e). All three challenge problems are corrected as extraction uncertainties; their underlying missing details remain in open_items, and none affects the final eligibility decision. open_items.item: Open question 1 and unresolved reconciliation difference studies.S1.participants.population: recruitment, population, country, and physical setting. Author recruitment and administration details would settle the metadata. None of the three eligibility criteria requires a particular population or setting, and random assignment is explicit.

Open question 2: original randomized counts and timing, reasons, and arm distribution of exclusions. An author allocation/attrition ledger would distinguish the seven exclusions from later screening. This affects participant-flow extraction; random assignment and a sample above the threshold are already supported.

Open question 3: exact analyzed total and arm denominators versus F(4, 237). Author model-specific sample counts and analysis specifications would settle the discrepancy. The exact n is unresolved, but the reported participant sample and participant-score ANOVA degrees of freedom both support criterion 2 well above 50.

Open question 4: continued Early-AI access during Round 2. The author protocol or task-interface access rules would settle with_ai versus after_ai for those final outputs. Late-AI suggestions are explicitly supplied during final production, so no eligibility criterion depends on this uncertainty.

Open question 5: expert-score aggregation, Round 1 rating procedure, and missing arm SDs, pairwise estimates, precision, and model-specific counts. Author scoring/analysis procedures and participant-level summaries would settle extraction. Criterion 3 already holds because experts explicitly rate produced submissions; exact standardization is not an eligibility requirement.

Open question 6: cosine-similarity transformation and aggregation across supplied suggestions. Author computation code or formula would settle the semantic-distance measure. The source establishes that it compares participant text with AI suggestions, and expert-rated creative output independently satisfies criterion 3.

Open question 7: Late-AI arm/aggregation behind the reported round changes and the conflict between Section 4.4 and Figure 2e about which group gained most in creativity. Author confirmation of the group labels and change analysis would settle the result attribution; effect magnitude and direction do not determine eligibility.

Open question 8: pilot n units, possible overlap with S1, and source of the stimulus-prerating mean. Author pilot methods and participant linkage would settle these details. The pilot is a stimulus check, contributes no eligible human-production outcome, and is not added to the independently qualifying main experiment.
